title: Everest Statements in Elementary School?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Responding to a question from an elementary teacher in Saudi Arabia about whether Everest Statements — the one-sentence distillations of a course's purpose that Stuart describes in These 6 Things — can work in elementary classrooms, Dave Stuart Jr. adapts the concept for self-contained elementary settings where one teacher covers multiple subjects. He outlines two workable approaches: a single overarching Everest Statement that has touchpoints across every subject taught, versus several subject-specific statements tailored to each block, citing his own ELA statement and math educator Caroline Ong's statement as examples. He frames the underlying goal as creating clarity of purpose for both teacher and students, arguing that without such clarity, frustration, distraction, and wasted time inevitably follow. The piece is a short, direct application of an established Stuart concept to a new grade-band context, prompted by reader correspondence.
points: Stuart offers two concrete elementary adaptations of the Everest Statement concept: one overarching cross-subject statement versus several subject-specific statements per block.
He cites his own ELA Everest Statement ("we are all about becoming better thinkers, readers, writers, speakers, and people") as a portable example elementary teachers could adapt.
He credits high school math educator Caroline Ong's statement ("Math is all about solving problems efficiently in a way you can communicate to others") as usable even at the elementary level.
His core claim is that clarity of purpose benefits both teacher and learner simultaneously, and that its absence reliably produces frustration, distraction, and time-wasting.
The article models Stuart's practice of adapting existing secondary-focused frameworks for elementary contexts based directly on reader questions.
quotes: I appreciate that These 6 Things is aimed at secondary teachers, but so much of it applies to elementary too! Do you have any examples of Everest Statements made by Elementary Teachers that you could share?

So first of all, when someone says "elementary," I am imagining a self-contained elementary classroom, where students are with the same teacher for most of the school day and are learning multiple subjects from that teacher.

I've heard of elementary teachers describing math using the same statement that Caroline Ong, a high school math educator, uses: Math is all about solving problems efficiently in a way you can communicate to others.
Both the teacher and the learners will perform best only when there is clarity of purpose. When those things are lacking, frustration and distraction and time-wasting will inevitably result.

An overarching Everest Statement — something that has touchpoints in all the subjects you are teaching. The colleague who wrote in had an example that would work wonderfully for this, as learning experiences and lessons in all kinds of subjects can nurture curiosity, create challenge, and allow for clear expression.
